docs.title: WP Updates Notifier
docs.text:
A free, open source, extensible, developer-friendly, accessible and security-conscious update notifier for WordPress.

WP Updates Notifier checks your site on a schedule and emails you when WordPress core, a plugin or a theme has an update waiting, so you know without logging in. It is made for sites you rarely visit and for sites you look after for clients.

Install from WordPress.org Read the user guide Read the developer guide View the code on GitHub

docs.title: Why WP Updates Notifier
docs.text:
• Free and open source

    GPL-2.0-or-later and developed in the open on GitHub. No tracking, no analytics and no account to sign up for.

  • Extensible

    A public, versioned API lets add-ons bring their own notification channels, item types, routing rules and configuration sources.

    Writing a module

  • Developer friendly

    Every hook is documented, settings can come from constants and environment variables, and the Docker setup runs every test with one make command.

    Hook reference

  • Accessible

    The settings screen is checked against WCAG 2.2 AA with axe and keyboard tests on every change. This site is checked the same way, in both colour schemes.

  • Security conscious

    A published threat model, security tests for every request handler, static and taint analysis in CI, and signed releases with build provenance you can verify.

    Threat model

  • Quietly useful

    Each new version is reported once, not every day. Choose the schedule, the recipients and whether to watch only the plugins and themes you have active.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Checks for core, plugin and theme updates hourly, twice daily, daily or weekly, and tells you about each new version once.
  • Sends email to one or more addresses, with a test send to check it arrives.
  • Can watch only active plugins and themes.
  • Lets you set channels and global settings in code: wp-config.php constants, environment variables or your own configuration source, so a fleet of sites can share one setup.
  • Routes each kind of update to the channels that should hear about it, and add-ons can add new kinds.

Requires WordPress 6.7 or newer and PHP 7.4 or newer.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
• WordPress.org (recommended): search for "WP Updates Notifier" under Plugins → Add New, or download it from wordpress.org/plugins/wp-updates-notifier.
  • Composer: through WordPress Packagist: composer require wpackagist-plugin/wp-updates-notifier.
  • Zip: each GitHub release has the plugin zip attached.

Then open Settings → Updates Notifier to choose where notifications go.

docs.title: Decision records
docs.text:
These are short records of decisions that shape WP Updates Notifier: what was decided, why, and what it costs. They exist so the reasons outlive the issue threads they came from.

A record is not a plan or a specification. It describes a decision that has been made. If a decision changes, the old record stays, its status says which record replaced it, and a new record explains the change.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
Each record is a file named NNNN-short-title.md, numbered in the order the records were written. It has:

  • a title, # NNNN. Title;
  • a line with the status (Accepted, or Superseded by a later record) and the date of the decision;
  • Context: the problem and what forced a choice;
  • Decision: what was chosen;
  • Consequences: the good and the bad;
  • Considered options, where there were real alternatives;
  • References: the issues and pull requests where the decision was made.

The date is when the decision was made, not when the record was written.

docs.title: 0001. Licence the plugin GPL-2.0-or-later
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-13.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The plugin stated its licence three ways. The plugin header said GPL3+, readme.txt said GPLv3 or later and composer.json said GPL-2.0-or-later. There was no LICENSE file. The licence notice in the code, which is the grant contributors' code was submitted under, says "either version 2 of the License, or (at your option) any later version".

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The plugin is licensed GPL-2.0-or-later. The repository has a LICENSE file with the full GPL version 2 text, and the plugin header, readme.txt and composer.json all say the same. A contract test checks that they agree.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: the licence matches the grant in the code and the WordPress.org norm.
  • Good: users can still choose GPLv3, because of "or later".
  • Bad: the plugin header and readme.txt change from GPL3+ wording, which is a visible change in 2.0.0.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text: • GPL-3.0-or-later. This was what the header and readme.txt said. It does not match the notice that contributors' code was submitted under, so it was rejected.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • #124: the licence file and consistent licence statements.

docs.title: 0002. Require PHP 7.4 and WordPress 6.7
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-12.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The plugin declared no PHP requirement. readme.txt still said Requires at least: 3.1 and Tested up to: 5.3, so WordPress.org showed its warning about plugins not tested with the latest three major releases. WordPress itself requires PHP 7.4 or later.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Version 2.0.0 requires PHP 7.4 (tested through 8.5) and WordPress 6.7. The plugin header, readme.txt and composer.json state the minimums. WordPress refuses to activate or update the plugin on older environments, so there is no runtime check.

WordPress 6.7 gives wp_get_wp_version() in place of the $wp_version global, and the 6.7 rules for loading translations at the right time. Everything else the plugin needs is older.

The code uses typed properties and ??, and avoids syntax newer than PHP 7.4 (match, union types, constructor promotion, the nullsafe operator, named arguments). This is a breaking change, so the commits use refactor! or feat! with a BREAKING CHANGE: footer, and the release is a major version.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: modern syntax, and one supported range to test.
  • Good: WordPress.org no longer warns that the plugin is untested.
  • Bad: sites below the minimum stay on 1.6.0, because WordPress.org does not offer them the update.
  • Bad: CI has to test PHP 7.4 to 8.5 against WordPress 6.7, the current release and trunk.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • #50: require PHP 7.4 and WordPress 6.7.

docs.title: 0003. Rename the main file without a migration stub
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-17.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The main file was class-sc-wp-updates-notifier.php, a class-file name. The conventional main file for the slug is wp-updates-notifier.php, which it was up to 1.4.4.

WordPress stores active plugins by path. When a plugin's main file is renamed, WordPress deactivates it on every site that updates. That happened when 1.5 renamed it away from wp-updates-notifier.php. A major version does not stop the update: WordPress.org offers it like any other.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Version 2.0.0 renames the main file to wp-updates-notifier.php and ships no migration stub. Sites that update from 1.5 or 1.6 find the plugin deactivated and must activate it again. Their settings are kept, and activation schedules the check again. Sites still on 1.4.x already have the new path stored and stay active.

The readme's 2.0.0 upgrade notice tells users to activate the plugin again. The commit is refactor! with a BREAKING CHANGE: footer, so the changelog lists it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: no stub, no active_plugins rewriting and no tests for them, carried until the next major version for a one-off step.
  • Good: the main file has the name people expect.
  • Bad: sites on 1.5 or 1.6 that update in the background lose their update notices until someone activates the plugin. This is the failure the plugin exists to prevent, and it was accepted for one release.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• A header-less stub at the old path. It would replace the old path with the new one in active_plugins (and active_sitewide_plugins on multisite) as soon as it loaded, then load the new main file. WordPress loads active files without a plugin header, and only later validates the list, so it would have kept every site active. It was the first plan. The maintainer decided against it because 2.0.0 is already a breaking release, and the stub, its migration and its tests would be carried until 3.0.0.
  • Keep the old file name. This avoids the problem and leaves a non-standard main file.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• #90: the rename, with the decision recorded in a comment.
  • PR #158: the implementation.

docs.title: 0004. A public, versioned module API, used by the built-in modules
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-12.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Version 1.x sent email and Slack from fixed code. Site owners and agencies wanted other channels, several channels at once, and different rules per channel. The plugin could not offer those without other plugins being able to add channels, and without a promise about what stays stable.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Notification channels are modules that register through a public hook, sc_wpun_register_channels. A site can have several instances of a module, each with its own routing. The hooks, the module classes and the field schema are public API, with their own semantic version (SC_WPUN_API_VERSION).

The built-in modules use only that API. Each lives in modules/<type>/, registers through the public hook and touches no internal classes. make check-public-api fails CI if a module reaches inside. If a module needs something that is not public, the API grows.

Add-ons state the API versions they work with as a Composer-style constraint, such as ^1.0. A header on the Plugins screen, a function and the channel class all take one, and the registry enforces the last. The stability and deprecation policy says what is public and how it changes.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: the built-in email module is a working example, and the API is tested by real use.
  • Good: add-on authors have a written promise, and a way to check it.
  • Bad: the plugin has to keep the public surface stable, deprecate before removing and bump the API version.
  • Bad: internal convenience is sometimes given up, because a module cannot use an internal class.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text: • Built-in modules that use internal classes, with the public API for add-ons only. Simpler for the built-ins, but the API would go unused by the plugin itself and could drift from what the built-ins need.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• #91: the epic.
  • #92: the module API, registry and dispatcher.
  • #105: contract tests and the check that modules use only the public API.
  • #106: the developer guide.
  • #189, #190 and #191: API version constraints.

docs.title: 0005. Keep settings, run state and channels in separate options
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-12.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
In 1.x the settings and the run state (the versions already notified, and the time of the last check) shared one autoloaded option, sc_wpun_settings. Every cron run rewrote the whole array several times. A settings save that overlapped a cron run could be overwritten by the cron's stale copy. The run state also went through the settings sanitiser.

The module system added a third kind of data: channel instances, each with its own settings and routing.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Each kind of data has its own option:

Option Holds Notes sc_wpun_settings The global settings Versioned by sc_wpun_settings_ver, which drives upgrades. sc_wpun_state The run state Not autoloaded, written once per run. sc_wpun_channels The channel instances Not autoloaded.

The 1.x email and Slack settings are migrated into channel instances once, and removed from sc_wpun_settings. The option names stay as they were wherever one existed, so older data and tools keep working.

The options are not public API. Add-ons read and write instances through sc_wpun_channels(), so the layout can change without breaking them (see stability).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: a settings save and a cron run no longer overwrite each other.
  • Good: the autoloaded option is small, and channel secrets are not autoloaded on every request.
  • Bad: three options to migrate, back up and clean up on uninstall.
  • Bad: code that read the old email and Slack keys from sc_wpun_settings directly stops working. This was recorded as a breaking change for 2.0.0.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• #75: settings and run state shared one option.
  • #93: channels as instances, and the 1.x migration.

docs.title: 0006. Drop Slack in 2.0.0 and keep its settings
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-14.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: About 30,000 sites run the plugin, and some rely on Slack for update alerts. Version 2.0.0 is a modernisation release focused on reliability and the new extension API, and it ships email as its only channel. Removing Slack quietly would stop those alerts with no warning, which is exactly what the plugin exists to prevent.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
2.0.0 sends no Slack notifications, but it does not delete anything:

  • The 1.x Slack settings are migrated into a slack channel instance, like any other, with its enabled flag.
  • 2.0.0 registers no slack module, so the dispatcher treats the instance as unavailable. It is skipped, reported and never deleted. If a module that provides the slack type is installed later, it resumes the instance with no reconfiguration.
  • Admins are told, once, in three places: a one-time email on the first run after the upgrade, a dismissible notice on the plugin's own settings screen only, and a Site Health item while a stored Slack instance exists. The email goes to the site's admin email if email notifications are off.
  • The wording is factual: what changed, what was kept, and that more notification channels are expected later.

The notice is includes/class-slack-notice.php.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: nobody loses their Slack settings, and nobody is left unaware that alerts stopped.
  • Good: the notice appears only on the plugin's screen, as WordPress.org guideline 11 asks.
  • Bad: sites that relied on Slack get no Slack alerts from 2.0.0 unless a module that provides the slack type is installed.
  • Bad: a stored but unusable instance is code and data to carry.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text: • Remove Slack and its settings. Simplest, but silent for the sites that depend on it.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• #143: drop Slack, keep its settings.
  • #93: the migration to instances.
  • #92: unavailable instances in the dispatcher.

docs.title: 0007. Allow settings and secrets from outside the database
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-12.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Site builders and agencies want configuration in code or in the environment, not in the database. This matters most for secrets such as webhook URLs, bot tokens and API keys, which should not sit in wp_options. It applies to any setting.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
For every global setting and every field of a channel instance, the plugin looks for a value in this order:

  1. wp-config.php constants. Always on.
  2. Environment variables. Opt-in, by setting SC_WPUN_LOAD_FROM_ENV, so variables a host happens to set never change behaviour by surprise.
  3. Sources added by add-ons, through the sc_wpun_config_sources filter. This is how a secrets service such as Vault can plug in.

The first source with a value wins. The sc_wpun_config_value filter then sees the result and has the last word. If nothing supplies a value, the one saved in the database is used.

Values from outside go through the same sanitisers and validators as saved ones. The settings screen shows them as read-only and says where they came from. The names are SC_WPUN_SETTING_<SETTING> and SC_WPUN_CHANNEL_<ID>__<FIELD>, and are public API. See Configuration sources.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: secrets can stay out of the database and out of backups of it.
  • Good: a deployment can pin settings, and add-ons can bring their own sources.
  • Bad: the screen and the stored value can disagree, so the screen has to say where a value came from.
  • Bad: instance IDs have to be constant-safe slugs that cannot change, because they form part of the names.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text: • Environment variables always on. Rejected, because stray host variables could change behaviour.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • #107: load settings and secrets from constants, environment variables or custom sources.

docs.title: 0008. Support single sites only in 2.0.0
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-17.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: On multisite, a network-activated plugin runs once per site. Each site has its own settings page, cron event and notification, so one update produces one email per site. A proper fix needs a network admin screen, one cron event on the main site, network-level settings and channel instances, and changes to activation and uninstall. That is a feature of its own, and it touches the settings, channels and tests.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: 2.0.0 supports single sites. Multisite network support moves to 3.0.0. The local development stack will run a single-site and a multisite install side by side to prepare for it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: 2.0.0 stays focused on reliability and the extension API.
  • Good: network support gets designed once, on top of the module system.
  • Bad: on multisite, the duplicate emails per site remain in 2.0.0.
  • Bad: the multisite tests for the new features wait for 3.0.0.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• #85: multisite network admin support, now in the 3.0.0 milestone.
  • #176: run single-site and multisite local sites side by side.

docs.title: 0009. No lock against overlapping update checks
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-18.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The action sc_wpun_run_check lets site code run the update check on demand. A manual run can overlap a scheduled one. Both can find the same new update and send it before either records it as notified, so a notice can arrive twice.

The first plan took a short lock around every check. Making it atomic is hard in WordPress: options need cache handling, and transients are not atomic.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: There is no lock. The worst outcome of an overlap is a duplicate update notice, and that is rare. The trade-off is documented in the architecture page and in Writing a module. A channel that must never deliver the same message twice keeps its own record in send().

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: less code and fewer ways for a stuck lock to stop checks.
  • Good: a manual run behaves exactly like a scheduled one.
  • Bad: an occasional duplicate notice.
  • Bad: channels with exactly-once needs carry the cost themselves.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text: • A lock using a transient or an option with an expiry. Rejected as a lot of plumbing for a rare, harmless outcome.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• #187: the public action to run the check, with the scope change in a comment.
  • PR #198: the implementation.

docs.title: 0010. Leave WordPress's own auto-update emails alone
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-19.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
1.x had an "Automatic updates" setting that rewrote the email WordPress sends after a core auto-update, sending it to the plugin's notification address. It covered core only, because plugin and theme auto-update emails still went to the admin email. With channels, "the notification address" is a guess: there may be no email channel, several, or a switched-off one. It also changed WordPress's default behaviour.

An issue to route plugin and theme auto-update emails the same way was open.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The plugin reports available updates through its channels and does not touch WordPress's own emails. The notify_automatic setting and the hook on auto_core_update_email are removed. WordPress sends these emails to the site admin email. An admin who wants them elsewhere changes that email, or uses the auto_core_update_email and auto_plugin_theme_update_email filters. The request to route plugin and theme emails was closed as not planned.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: less code, and WordPress behaves as documented.
  • Good: no rule is needed to pick an email channel.
  • Bad: a breaking change for sites that used the setting. Their core auto-update emails now go to the admin email.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• #262: stop redirecting core auto-update emails.
  • #84: route plugin and theme auto-update emails, closed as not planned.

docs.title: 0011. Settings screen to WCAG 2.2 AA, without JavaScript
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-18.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A review of the settings screen, the field markup that modules get for free, the notices and the notifications found gaps against WCAG 2.2 level AA. Many were small, such as page titles, error messages and heading structure. Two needed a choice: whether an error summary should rely on JavaScript, and what markup the channels list should use.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The settings screen and the notifications meet WCAG 2.2 AA. The admin UI needs no JavaScript: for example, a failed form gets an "Error:" page title and an error summary that is announced without script. The channels list follows core's WP_List_Table pattern.

CI checks this. make a11y runs axe (WCAG 2.2 A and AA) and keyboard tests against a throwaway site, as a required check. A person still checks new markup by keyboard and with a screen reader.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: the screen works for keyboard and screen reader users, and with scripts blocked.
  • Good: modules get accessible field markup without extra work.
  • Bad: automated checks catch only part of WCAG, so manual checks stay necessary.
  • Bad: some interactions are plainer than script would allow.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• #206: the accessibility review epic.
  • PR #264: the fixes and make a11y.

docs.title: 0012. Security tooling is free, deterministic and scripted
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-18.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Every build, from a pull request to the zip on WordPress.org, should be checked for security problems. Checks that give different answers locally and in CI, or on different days, cannot be trusted as a gate.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Security checks are free, deterministic tools run from scripts:

  • Everything runs through make in Docker, with a target and a CI job for each tool.
  • Tool versions are pinned (image digest or action SHA) and Dependabot bumps them. Rules live in the repo and are never fetched at run time.
  • Findings fail the build. Each suppression carries a one-line reason. A baseline may only shrink.
  • A real secret found anywhere is rotated, never baselined.
  • No AI in the CI loop. One AI-assisted review is run by hand and is advisory, not a gate. Each finding it confirms becomes a deterministic test or rule.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: the same result locally and in CI, and no cost per run.
  • Good: a fixed issue stays fixed without anyone repeating the review.
  • Bad: the pinned tools need regular bumps.
  • Bad: the tools find known patterns only. The hand-run review and the threat model cover what rules miss.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• #229: the security epic.
  • #230: the advisory AI-assisted review.

docs.title: 0013. Make releases verifiable
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-19.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
A checksum published next to the zip proves only that the download was not corrupted. It does not show that the zip came from this repository's CI at a given commit. If a release job or a maintainer's machine were compromised, users and WordPress.org could not tell.

release-please creates tags through the API, and those tags are unsigned.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A release produces a zip that can be checked:

  • Reproducible zip. make dist-repro builds it twice and fails if the SHA-256 values differ. CI runs it on every pull request.
  • SBOM. A CycloneDX software bill of materials, attached to the release.
  • Build provenance. The zip and the SBOM are attested, and gh attestation verify checks them.
  • Signed annotated tags. The release job creates the vX.Y.Z tag itself, signed with a dedicated key in the release environment.
  • release-please prepares a Release PR and a draft release. The release job waits for the maintainer's approval, then builds, attests, tags and publishes. See CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: anyone can check that a zip came from this repository's CI at a given commit.
  • Good: nothing is published without the maintainer's approval.
  • Bad: more release machinery, and a signing key to protect.
  • Bad: the last acceptance check can only be done on the first real release.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text: • Rely on the attestation and leave tags unsigned. The attestation already ties the zip to the commit, but a signed tag shows who released it.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• #226: reproducible zip, provenance and SBOM.
  • PR #258: the release job and signed tags.
  • #57: deploy to WordPress.org on release.

docs.title: 0014. Publish the documentation at wpun.cariss.dev with MkDocs Material and mike
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-20.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The public API, the configuration sources and the settings need documentation that can be browsed per version, not one long readme. Released plugin versions link to the documentation, so the address has to outlive any change of hosting or repository name.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The documentation is a static site built from the Markdown in docs/, at https://wpun.cariss.dev.

  • A custom subdomain served by GitHub Pages, not l3rady.github.io. Links shipped in released plugins keep working if the hosting or the repository moves.
  • MkDocs Material, with mike for versions. main, each release, and a latest alias that becomes the default once the first release is out. Docs stay as one set of Markdown files, with no copy per version.
  • GitHub Pages deploys from the gh-pages branch. mike builds up every version there.
  • Pull requests build the site in strict mode, so broken links and pages missing from the navigation fail.
  • No tracking and no third-party requests, like the plugin itself.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: stable links, documentation per release, and checks on every pull request.
  • Bad: the domain and its DNS have to be kept.
  • Bad: Python tooling, run in Docker, alongside the PHP tooling.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Docusaurus. Versioning is built in, but it copies the whole docs folder for each version, and it needs React and Node.
  • VitePress or Starlight. No built-in versioning.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• #271: the website epic.
  • #156: the versioned documentation site.

docs.title: 0015. Conventional Commits and a linear history
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-13.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Releases are automated, and the version number and changelog have to come from somewhere reliable. Pull requests also need to land as clean history that is easy to read and bisect.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Every commit is a Conventional Commit. fix is a patch, feat a minor, and ! with a BREAKING CHANGE: footer a major. release-please builds the next version and CHANGELOG.md from them.
  • make commits checks the commits on a branch, and CI runs it on every pull request.
  • History is linear. Branches rebase onto main, and main is never merged into a branch.
  • Pull requests land as their own commits, not squashed, so the commit messages that decide the version are the ones on main.
  • Commits are signed. Since 2026-10-19 the maintainer merges a pull request by rebasing it onto main and fast-forwarding main locally, so the signed commits land unchanged. GitHub's rebase and squash buttons rewrite the commits, so the maintainer's own signatures would not reach main.

See CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: versions and the changelog follow from the history, with no manual step.
  • Good: a linear history is easy to follow.
  • Bad: contributors have to write commit messages with care, and rebase instead of merging.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • PR #119: automate releases with release-please.

docs.title: 0016. Remind about pending updates, per channel
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-23.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Version 1.4.4 emailed about every waiting update on every check. Version 1.6 reports each version once, which stopped the repeated emails but also removed the nudge: an update nobody installs is never mentioned again. Users asked for the old behaviour back, for example in the forum thread "How to get old behavior of daily e-mail notification" (2020), and an earlier pull request, #13 (add-resend-updates-setting), tried a global setting.

Since 2.0.0 there are several channel instances, each with its own routing. A reminder has to fit that: someone may want a weekly email to the site owner and nothing for a chat channel.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• A per-channel routing key. remind is never (the default), daily or weekly. It lives in the instance's routing, so channels defined in code can set it too, and no settings version changes.
  • A clock in the run state. channels[id][last_reminder] in sc_wpun_state is the time the interval started or the last reminder was sent. It starts when something first waits for the instance, so the first reminder comes one interval later, and it is cleared when nothing waits or the setting is never. A skip run starts it too, so skipped updates are reminded about later.
  • One message, every waiting item. A reminder lists everything waiting for the instance and is marked with Notification::is_reminder(). The built-in renderers and the email subject say so.
  • Fold rule. A new update found in the same check as a due reminder goes in the reminder. There is one message, not two. A new update between reminders is sent at once, as before, and does not touch the clock.
  • Tolerance. A reminder is due when the time since the last one is at least the interval minus half the check frequency's interval, with that tolerance capped at half the reminder interval. WP-Cron runs late on quiet sites and the next run is scheduled from the planned time, so a strict comparison would make a daily reminder on a daily check skip a cycle.
  • A failed reminder does not move the clock and is tried again at the next check.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: the old behaviour is available again, without the noise for people who did not ask for it.
  • Good: it needs no new cron event, hook or lock. It reuses the update check.
  • Bad: reminders follow the check frequency, so they can not be more frequent than checks. Weekly checks mean a daily reminder goes on every check.
  • Bad: modules see one more kind of message. A reminder lists items that were delivered before, so a module that de-duplicates by item must not drop them. The module guide says so.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• A global setting, as in #13. Rejected: routing is already per instance, and "weekly to email only" is a real need.
  • A separate cron event for reminders. Rejected: it adds scheduling to maintain, and the check already runs.
  • Two messages in the same run, a reminder and a message for new updates. Rejected: it is noise.
  • Postponing the reminder when something new arrives. Rejected: on a busy site the reminder could be postponed for ever.
  • A strict interval. Rejected: cron drift would make reminders skip a cycle.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Issue #81: optional reminders for updates still pending.
  • Old pull request #13 (add-resend-updates-setting), which proposed a global setting.
  • Issue #75 and issue #95: the run state option and the per-channel routing and delivery state that reminders build on.

docs.title: 0017. Bundle translations as .l10n.php files only
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-24.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
WordPress 6.5 added performant translations: a .l10n.php file is loaded in preference to the .mo file next to it. The plugin needs WordPress 6.7, so every supported site prefers .l10n.php.

translate.wordpress.org builds a language pack for a locale once about 90% of the release's strings are translated, and WordPress installs packs per locale into wp-content/languages/plugins. Core resolves one languages directory per text domain and locale, with the packs first. The old 1.x packs (de_DE, de_DE_formal, es_ES, ja, pl_PL, da_DK and en_GB) would therefore hide a complete bundled file for those locales.

The first version of the bundled translations committed a .pot, a .po, a .mo and a .l10n.php file for each of 11 locales: about 1.1 MB in the zip, and four files to keep in step.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Bundle 11 locales, made in Claude Code sessions: de_DE, fr_FR, es_ES, it_IT, nl_NL, pt_BR, ja, ru_RU, pl_PL, zh_CN and he_IL. The other 19 locales are tracked in #299.
  • Commit and ship only languages/wp-updates-notifier-<locale>.l10n.php. There is no committed .pot, .po or .mo. The .l10n.php file is the source of truth, and the gettext files are generated into the git-ignored build/translations/ when a translating session needs them (make translations-edit).
  • The loader points WordPress at the bundled directory for the locales the plugin ships. It loads an installed language pack first, so the pack's strings win, and the bundled file fills the gaps. A pack counts in either format, as packs are external.
  • The translations are machine-made and unreviewed until they are imported to translate.wordpress.org, which needs a project translation editor (#58). The .l10n.php format cannot carry a marker, so the documentation records this.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: the zip carries about 320 KB of translations instead of about 1.1 MB, and there is one file per locale to keep in step.
  • Good: translators lose nothing, as translate.wordpress.org scans the code for strings itself. This supersedes the committed .pot of #61.
  • Bad: a site that forces the MO format with the translation_file_format filter gets no bundled strings.
  • Bad: any change to a string or translators comment fails CI until a translation session runs make translations-edit, fills the empty entries, and runs make translations.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Keep the .po and .mo files too. Rejected: they triple the size and add files that can drift from the .l10n.php, for sites that force a format WordPress no longer prefers.
  • Ship only the .po and let sites build. Rejected: WordPress cannot read a .po file.
  • Rely on language packs alone. Rejected: packs exist for a few locales, are partial, and wait for the translations to be imported.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Issue #147: bundled translations.
  • Issue #61: the translation template.
  • Issue #58: a project translation editor on translate.wordpress.org.
  • Issue #299: the remaining locales.

docs.title: 0018. Generate readme.txt at build time and do not commit it
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-10-25.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
readme.txt repeated facts that live elsewhere: the plugin header (name, requirements, licence, version), CHANGELOG.md, the user guide on wpun.cariss.dev and the links on the About tab. Kept by hand it drifted. It still listed 1.x features, named a settings page that no longer exists, and its changelog stopped at 1.6. bin/set-stable-tag.sh patched one line of it on the Release PR, and the Release PR only worked because nobody else touched the file.

WordPress.org reads readme.txt or readme.md, and both must use the WordPress readme format, so README.md (the GitHub page) cannot serve. The file has to exist in the zip, the SVN deploy and the GitHub release asset, and all three must carry the same one.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• readme.txt is not committed. It is in .gitignore. bin/readme.php generates it, bin/build-dist.sh writes it into build/wp-updates-notifier/ after copying the tracked files, and so the zip, the SVN deploy and the release asset carry the same file. make readme writes a preview to build/readme.txt, never to the repository root.
  • The inputs are committed files. .wordpress-org/readme/template.txt holds the hand-written text and the fields that cannot be derived (contributors, tags, tested up to). The plugin header gives the name, requirements, licence and the stable tag (the version). About_Tab::links() gives the donate link, so the readme, the About tab and the home page cannot disagree. CHANGELOG.md gives the latest 3 releases. The FAQ comes from the ## headings of docs/users/troubleshooting.md that .wordpress-org/readme/faq.txt lists, followed by the questions only the readme has.
  • It is reproducible. The generator reads nothing that varies (no date, locale, environment or network), so make dist-repro covers it, and the attestation and SBOM describe what ships.
  • It fails rather than guess. A listed FAQ heading that is missing, or Markdown the generator cannot render, stops the build.
  • make check-headers checks the generated file against WordPress.org's rules: the title, the required fields and their agreement with the plugin header, the stable tag, at most 5 tags, a short description of at most 150 characters, only known sections, Upgrade Notice entries of at most 300 characters, and no placeholder left.
  • The Release PR no longer sets a stable tag. The release workflow only sets the copyright year.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good: the version, requirements, licence, changelog and FAQ have one source each, and the readme cannot go stale.
  • Good: no generated file in the repository, so no staleness check and no merge conflicts in it.
  • Good: the FAQ answers are the ones on the documentation site, so they are written once.
  • Bad: a reader of the repository cannot open readme.txt or see its diff in a pull request. make readme shows it, and a change to a source shows in the diff of the source.
  • Bad: anything that needs the readme must build it first. Lychee (make docs-links) and the WordPress tests (they call the generator) do; the release deploy to SVN (#57) takes it from the zip.
  • Bad: the FAQ and changelog Markdown support is the subset the user guide uses. A new construct needs the generator taught first.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Commit a generated readme.txt with a make check-readme staleness check. This was the first plan. It keeps a file the zip is built from git ls-files with, allows a readme-only deploy straight from git, and shows the diff in review. Rejected because the maintainer wants no generated file in the repository, and the build directory carries the generated file to every channel anyway.
  • Keep readme.txt by hand. Rejected: it drifted, which is the problem.
  • Ship readme.md instead. Rejected: WordPress.org prefers readme.txt and both need the same format.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Issue #282: generate readme.txt.
  • Issue #283: the donate link and the Author URI.
  • Issue #57: the WordPress.org deploy.
  • Issue #59: the readme text.

docs.title: Developer guide
docs.text:
WP Updates Notifier 2.0.0 and later can be extended by other plugins: new notification channels, new kinds of item to report, routing rules, and places to read settings and secrets from. Everything here uses the public API, which follows the stability and deprecation policy.

  • Architecture: how an update check flows from WP-Cron to each channel instance, and where your code plugs in.
  • Writing a notification module: a channel type step by step: field schema, validation, secrets, send(), Delivery_Result, rate and length limits, and testing with mocked HTTP.
  • Item types and routing: reporting something other than core, plugin and theme updates, and deciding which instances receive it.
  • Configuration sources: settings and secrets from wp-config.php constants, environment variables or a secrets service.
  • Hook reference: every action and filter, generated from the code.
  • Stability and deprecation: what is public, how it changes, and how an add-on checks the API version with a version constraint.
  • Tests and checks: the test layers, what each one catches, and the make target and CI job for each.
  • Translations: the bundled locales, how the files are made and checked, and what to do when a string changes.
  • Decision records: why the plugin is built the way it is, such as the licence, the minimum versions, the module system and what was dropped.
  • Threat model: what the plugin trusts, its entry points, and the control and test for each. The security rules for add-ons are in Writing a module (secrets, HTTP, and running the plugin's checks on your code).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• examples/wpun-example-channel/: a complete, minimal channel add-on to copy. CI runs its tests (tests/wp/test-example-channel.php) and checks it uses only the public API.
  • modules/email/: the built-in email channel, written like any add-on.
  • tests/fixtures/plugins/wpun-test-addon/: the add-on the test suite uses to exercise every extension point.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
This page follows one update check from start to finish, so you know where your code plugs in.

flowchart TD
    cron["WP-Cron: sc_wpun_update_check"] --> check["Update check<br>core, plugins, themes"]
    check --> items["Notification_Item list<br>filter: sc_wpun_update_items"]
    items --> veto["Global veto<br>filter: sc_wpun_should_notify_item"]
    veto --> notification["Notification<br>filter: sc_wpun_notification"]
    notification --> instances["Each enabled Channel_Instance"]
    instances --> routing["Routing<br>types, scope, core<br>filter: sc_wpun_channel_should_receive_item"]
    routing --> dedupe["Drop items this instance<br>was already told about"]
    dedupe --> dispatcher["Dispatcher<br>filter: sc_wpun_pre_send"]
    dispatcher --> send["Channel::send()"]
    send --> result["Delivery_Result<br>actions: sc_wpun_notification_sent / _failed"]
    result --> state["Run state saved per instance<br>action: sc_wpun_after_update_check"]

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
Update check. WP-Cron runs the sc_wpun_update_check event at the frequency chosen on the settings screen. You can also run it on demand with do_action( 'sc_wpun_run_check' ): it works like a scheduled run, the notification's source is manual instead of cron, and the schedule is not changed. There is no lock between runs, by design: if a manual run overlaps a scheduled one, both can send the same update before either records it, so a notification can arrive twice. That is rare and harmless for update notices, so the plugin keeps the check simple. A channel that must never deliver twice can keep its own record of what it sent. The check asks WordPress for core, plugin and theme updates and turns each one into a WPUN\Notification_Item. The global settings decide what is looked at: WordPress updates (none, all or only major releases), plugins and themes (none, all or only active ones).

Items. A Notification_Item is one thing waiting for an update: its type (core, plugin, theme or a type an add-on registers), a key that identifies it within the type (the plugin file, the theme stylesheet or core), a name, the installed and the available version, links, notes and machine-readable flags such as active. Add-ons can add their own items with the sc_wpun_update_items filter. See Item types and routing.

Global veto. sc_wpun_should_notify_item can stop an item from being reported anywhere. A vetoed item still counts as waiting, so its history is kept.

Notification. The items are wrapped in a WPUN\Notification with the site name, the site URL, the link to the Updates screen and some context, such as whether this is a test message. The sc_wpun_notification filter can change it before any channel sees it.

Channels and instances. A channel is a kind of delivery (the built-in email, or one your add-on registers) and is a subclass of WPUN\Channel. An instance is one configured use of a channel, for example "email to the ops team", stored as a WPUN\Channel_Instance with an id, a label, an enabled flag, its field values and its routing. Site owners create instances on the Channels tab. Instances can also be defined in code with the SC_WPUN_CHANNELS constant or the sc_wpun_channels filter. Channels are registered on the sc_wpun_register_channels action. A channel that declares an API version the site does not have (get_api_constraint()) is refused: it is not registered, sc_wpun_channel_rejected fires, and the Channels tab, a notice on the settings page and Site Health say why. Its instances are kept, but nothing is sent through them.

Routing. Each instance receives only the items its routing allows: which item types, all or only active plugins and themes, and all or only major WordPress releases. The sc_wpun_channel_should_receive_item filter adds rules of your own.

Delivery state. The plugin remembers, per instance, which version of each item it has told that instance about, and when it last sent a reminder. An instance is sent only what is new to it. If a send fails, nothing is recorded for that instance, so the same items go out again on the next run, while the instances that succeeded are not sent them twice.

Reminders. The remind routing key (never, daily or weekly) turns on reminders for an instance. The state of an instance has a last_reminder (a unix time) in sc_wpun_state, under channels[id]:

  • While remind is not never and the instance receives at least one waiting item, the clock runs. The first check that sees this sets last_reminder to now and sends no reminder, so the first one comes one interval later. When remind is never or nothing is waiting, last_reminder is removed.
  • A reminder is due when now - last_reminder is at least the interval minus a tolerance. The tolerance is half the interval of the site's check frequency, capped at half the reminder interval, so a late WP-Cron run does not skip a cycle.
  • When it is due, the check sends one Notification with is_reminder() true and every waiting item the instance receives, even those that are new in this run. On success all of them are recorded as notified and last_reminder is set to now. On failure neither changes, so the next check tries again.
  • Between reminders, new items are sent as a normal message and the clock is untouched. A skip run (see State::skip_pending()) sends no reminder but starts the clock. An instance that is off or deferred by retry_at is not touched. A test send never goes through the clock.

There is no separate cron event. Reminders can not be more frequent than the check frequency.

Dispatcher. The dispatcher calls your channel's send() for one instance and turns whatever happens into a WPUN\Delivery_Result. It catches exceptions, so a broken add-on cannot stop the other channels. An instance whose channel is not registered fails as unavailable, with the reason if the module was refused for its API version. sc_wpun_pre_send can short-circuit a send. sc_wpun_notification_sent and sc_wpun_notification_failed fire after each one, and sc_wpun_after_dispatch after all of them.

Results. The last result of each instance is shown on the Channels tab. Once every instance has had its turn, the run state is saved and sc_wpun_after_update_check fires.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Global settings live in the sc_wpun_settings option, the instances in sc_wpun_channels and the delivery state in sc_wpun_state. Read instances through sc_wpun_channels(), not the option, so instances defined in code and values from configuration sources are included. Any setting or channel field can instead come from a wp-config.php constant, an environment variable or a source your add-on registers. See Configuration sources.

docs.title: Public and internal code
docs.text: Everything in includes/ is in the WPUN namespace. Classes and methods tagged @internal are not part of the public API and can change in any release. Everything else that is documented with @since is public; see Stability and deprecation. The built-in email module in modules/email/ uses only the public API, and CI (make check-public-api) makes sure it stays that way.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Trust boundaries. Requests to admin-post.php and options.php, plugin and theme headers, data from api.wordpress.org, and the responses of the services a channel sends to are untrusted. Code in the same PHP process, add-ons included, is trusted, so the API keeps add-ons safe when used as documented but doesn't sandbox them.
  • Capability and security token. Every screen and handler checks current_user_can() with the capability from sc_wpun_capability (manage_options by default), then a security token for that action (wp_verify_nonce()). Row actions bind the token to the channel id. There are no nopriv handlers, and the security tests discover every handler and try it with each role and bad token.
  • Output. Values are escaped late, for the context they are printed in. Update data passes through Notification_Item, which keeps each value to one line, and then through Notification_Renderer, which escapes for HTML, plain text or Markdown.
  • Secrets. A secret field is never rendered, and never passed to a renderer. Channel_Instance and Config_Value hide values from var_dump() and print_r(). Secrets stay in the options table in plain text unless they come from a constant, an environment variable or a source (see Configuration sources).
  • Outbound requests. Addresses typed in by a site owner go through wp_safe_remote_*, which refuses private and loopback hosts.

The threat model lists every entry point and trust boundary. For each one it names the control and the test or tool that proves it.

docs.title: Configuration sources
docs.text: Any global setting and any field of a channel instance, including the fields of your own channel, can be supplied from outside the database. This keeps secrets such as webhook URLs and API tokens out of wp_options, and lets a deployment pin settings that the admin screen then shows as read-only.

docs.title: Where values come from
docs.text:
For each value the plugin asks, in order:

  1. wp-config.php constants. Always on.
  2. Environment variables. Only when the environment variable SC_WPUN_LOAD_FROM_ENV is 1, true, yes or on, or the sc_wpun_load_from_env filter returns true. This keeps variables a host happens to set from changing the plugin's behaviour.
  3. Sources added by add-ons, through the sc_wpun_config_sources filter.

The first source with a value wins. The sc_wpun_config_value filter then sees the result (or null) and has the last word. If nothing supplies a value, the one saved in the database is used.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
Constants and environment variables share the same names:

What Name Example A global setting SC_WPUN_SETTING_<SETTING> SC_WPUN_SETTING_FREQUENCY A field of a channel instance SC_WPUN_CHANNEL_<INSTANCE_ID>__<FIELD> SC_WPUN_CHANNEL_OPS_TEAM__WEBHOOK_URL

The instance id and the field name are upper-cased, with a double underscore between them. Instance ids are lower case letters and digits, in words joined by single underscores (ops_team), so every id makes a valid constant name.

Your channel's fields get these names automatically. You don't need to do anything to support them, but do say in your docs which fields are worth setting this way.

Whole instances can be defined in code too, with the SC_WPUN_CHANNELS constant (a JSON list) or the sc_wpun_channels filter. See the sc_wpun_channels entry in the hook reference.

docs.title: Values and types
docs.text:
Sources return scalars: a string, bool, int or float. The plugin casts the value to the type of the setting or field and runs it through the same validation as a value typed into the form. A value that fails is reported on the settings screen and in Site Health, and is not used.

  • A boolean field accepts 1, true, yes and on, or 0, false, no, off and an empty value, in any case.
  • An enum field takes the option key; a multiple-choice enum takes keys separated by commas, such as core,plugin.

docs.title: On the settings screen
docs.text: A value supplied from outside is read-only on the settings screen, which names where it came from ("Set by ..."). The screen never prints the value of a secret field, nor of a text-type field (text, textarea, url, email_list), unless that field sets 'show_external' => true. The built-in email channel does this for its recipients, From address, Reply-To and subject prefix. Booleans, numbers and enum choices are shown. Duplicating an instance doesn't copy secrets that came from outside the database. Reports and Site Health name the source of a rejected value, never the value.

docs.title: Hiding the About tab
docs.text:
The About tab of the settings screen (links to the documentation, support and the author) is shown unless you hide it. The show_about setting is code only: it has no field on the settings screen, it is never saved to the database, and a value posted from the form is ignored. Supply it like any other setting, with SC_WPUN_SETTING_SHOW_ABOUT; it takes the same boolean values as other on/off settings, and a value that is not valid is reported and the default (shown) is used.

// wp-config.php
define( 'SC_WPUN_SETTING_SHOW_ABOUT', false );

Or from a plugin, with the sc_wpun_config_value filter:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_config_value',
    function ( $value, $context ) {
        return 'show_about' === $context->get_setting() ? false : $value;
    },
    10,
    2
);

If you hide the tab, please consider a donation or a review in return.

docs.title: Writing a source
docs.text:
Implement WPUN\Config_Source and add an instance with sc_wpun_config_sources:

class My_Vault_Source implements \WPUN\Config_Source {

    public function get( string $key, \WPUN\Config_Context $context ) {
        // Only answer for the channel fields you manage.
        if ( \WPUN\Config_Context::SCOPE_CHANNEL !== $context->get_scope() ) {
            return null;
        }

        return my_vault_lookup( 'wpun/' . $key ); // A scalar, or null for "not here".
    }

    public function get_label( string $key ): string {
        return 'My Vault'; // Never include the value.
    }
}

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_config_sources',
    function ( $sources ) {
        $sources[] = new My_Vault_Source();
        return $sources;
    }
);

get() receives the constant-style name as $key and a WPUN\Config_Context that tells you what is being asked for:

  • get_scope(): Config_Context::SCOPE_SETTING or Config_Context::SCOPE_CHANNEL.
  • get_setting(): for a setting, its name, such as frequency.
  • get_instance_id() and get_field(): for a channel field.
  • get_site_id(): the site being configured.
  • get_key(): the same name as $key.

Rules for a source:

  • Return null when you have no value, so the next source is asked.
  • Never log, print or put the value in get_label(). It may be a secret. The plugin keeps values in WPUN\Config_Value objects, which hide the value from var_dump(), print_r() and serialisation.
  • A source may throw. The plugin records the class of the exception (not its message, which could contain a secret) and asks the next source.
  • Results are cached for the request, so get() is not called again for the same key.

The test add-on in tests/fixtures/plugins/wpun-test-addon/ has a working source.

docs.title: Hook reference
docs.text:
This file is generated from the doc blocks of the hooks the plugin fires. To change it, edit the doc block in the source and run make hook-docs. make check-hooks (part of the lint workflow) fails when this file is out of date.

Every hook is prefixed sc_wpun_. A name with a part in braces, such as sc_wpun_channel_payload_{type}, is dynamic: the part in braces is replaced when the hook fires.

  • Update check
  • Items and routing
  • Delivery
  • Channels and fields
  • Configuration
  • Settings screen
  • Lifecycle and legacy
  • Actions you can fire

docs.title: sc_wpun_after_update_check
docs.text:
Action, since 2.0.0

Fires when an update check has finished, after the state was saved.

It fires even if nothing was sent, with an empty $results.

Parameter Type Description $notification Notification The notification of the check, with every item that was waiting. $results array<string, Delivery_Result> Result by channel instance id, for the instances something was sent to.

Fired in includes/class-update-checker.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_before_update_check
docs.text:
Action, since 2.0.0

Fires when an update check starts, before anything is looked up.

Fired in includes/class-update-checker.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_frequencies
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters the names of the cron schedules offered as check frequencies.

Each must be a registered schedule (see the cron_schedules filter) of at least an hour.

Parameter Type Description $names string[] Schedule names. Default hourly, twicedaily, daily and weekly.

Fired in includes/class-frequencies.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_channel_should_receive_item
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters whether a channel instance receives an item, for rules of your own.

Runs after the instance's own rules, so it can veto an item the rules let through and allow one they blocked.

Example, send only plugins named "security" to the instance called "security_team":

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_channel_should_receive_item',
    function ( $receive, $item, $instance ) {
        if ( 'security_team' === $instance->get_id() && 'plugin' === $item->get_type() ) {
            return false !== stripos( $item->get_name(), 'security' );
        }
        return $receive;
    },
    10,
    3
);
Parameter Type Description $receive bool Whether the instance receives the item. $item Notification_Item The item. $instance Channel_Instance The instance.

Fired in includes/class-routing.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_core_needs_update
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters whether a WordPress core update is reported, like the plugin and theme filters do for theirs.

The default follows the "Notify about WordPress updates?" setting: true, or with "only major releases" whether the update is a major.minor change. Returning false reports no core item. What was already notified about core is kept while the update is waiting.

Example, ignore release candidates:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_core_needs_update',
    function ( $needs, $new_version ) {
        return $needs && false === strpos( $new_version, '-RC' );
    },
    10,
    2
);
Parameter Type Description $needs bool Whether to report the update. Default true, or whether it is a major release with "only major releases". $new_version string The version WordPress offers. $current_version string The installed version.

Fired in includes/class-update-checker.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_item_types
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters the item types, to register types of your own.

A type is a key of lower case letters, digits and underscores, with a label. Invalid entries are dropped, and core, plugin and theme cannot be removed or renamed away.

Example, register a type for PHP end-of-life warnings:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_item_types',
    function ( $types ) {
        $types['php'] = __( 'PHP', 'my-addon' );
        return $types;
    }
);
Parameter Type Description $types array<string, string> Type => label.

Fired in includes/class-item-types.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_notification
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters the notification built by the update check, before any channel instance gets its share.

Must return a Notification; anything else is ignored. Each instance then receives the items of the returned notification that its routing allows.

Example, drop the notes of every item:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_notification',
    function ( $notification ) {
        return $notification->with_items( my_strip_notes( $notification->get_items() ) );
    }
);
Parameter Type Description $notification Notification The notification, with every item that is waiting.

Fired in includes/class-update-checker.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_plugins_need_update
docs.text:
Filter, since 1.0.0

Filters the plugins that are waiting for an update and will be reported.

Parameter Type Description $plugins_need_update array<string, object> Update data from WordPress by plugin file (for example hello.php).

Fired in includes/class-update-checker.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_should_notify_item
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters whether an item is reported at all, to every channel instance.

An item that is vetoed is not sent and not recorded, but still counts as waiting for an update.

Example, never report one plugin:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_should_notify_item',
    function ( $notify, $item ) {
        return 'noisy/noisy.php' === $item->get_key() ? false : $notify;
    },
    10,
    2
);
Parameter Type Description $notify bool Whether to report the item. Default true. $item Notification_Item The item.

Fired in includes/class-update-checker.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_themes_need_update
docs.text:
Filter, since 1.0.0

Filters the themes that are waiting for an update and will be reported.

Parameter Type Description $themes_need_update array<string, array<string, mixed>> Update data from WordPress by theme stylesheet.

Fired in includes/class-update-checker.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_update_items
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters the items found by the check, to add, remove or change items.

Runs after core, plugins and themes were collected and before the global settings' routing. Only Notification_Item objects are kept. An item type other than core, plugin and theme must be registered with the sc_wpun_item_types filter for its history to be kept up to date: once no item of a registered type is returned, what was notified about it is forgotten.

Example, report an item of your own:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_update_items',
    function ( $items ) {
        $items[] = new \WPUN\Notification_Item(
            array(
                'type'            => 'php',
                'key'             => 'php',
                'name'            => 'PHP',
                'current_version' => PHP_VERSION,
                'new_version'     => '8.4',
            )
        );
        return $items;
    }
);
Parameter Type Description $items Notification_Item[] The items found, in the order of the message.

Fired in includes/class-update-checker.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_after_dispatch
docs.text:
Action, since 2.0.0

Fires when a round of delivery has finished: a dispatch, or an update check that sent something.

Parameter Type Description $results array<string, Delivery_Result> Result by channel instance id. $notification Notification The notification that was delivered.

Fired in includes/class-dispatcher.php, includes/class-update-checker.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_channel_payload
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters the payload of any channel just before it is sent.

The shape of the payload is up to the channel; see its documentation. The email channel uses array( 'to' => string[], 'subject' => string, 'message' => string, 'headers' => string[] ).

Example, add a recipient to every email:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_channel_payload',
    function ( $payload, $notification, $instance ) {
        if ( 'email' === $instance->get_type() ) {
            $payload['to'][] = 'archive@example.org';
        }
        return $payload;
    },
    10,
    3
);

$instance holds the resolved settings, secrets included: don't log or dump its settings.

Parameter Type Description $payload mixed The payload. $notification Notification What is being delivered. $instance Channel_Instance The instance it is delivered through.

Fired in includes/abstract-class-channel.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_channel_payload_{type}
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters the payload of the channels of one type just before it is sent.

The dynamic part, $type, is the channel type, for example email. The arguments are the same as for sc_wpun_channel_payload.

$instance holds the resolved settings, secrets included: don't log or dump its settings.

Parameter Type Description $payload mixed The payload. $notification Notification What is being delivered. $instance Channel_Instance The instance it is delivered through.

Fired in includes/abstract-class-channel.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_email_content
docs.text:
Filter, since 1.4.3. Since 2.0.0 also receives the notification and the instance, and is not HTML-escaped.

Filters the body of the email.

$instance holds the resolved settings, secrets included: don't log or dump its settings.

Parameter Type Description $body string Body: plain text, or HTML if the instance is set to HTML. An HTML body is a fragment: it is wrapped in a document with the language, direction and title after this filter. $notification Notification The notification. $instance Channel_Instance The instance sending it.

Fired in includes/class-notifier.php, modules/email/class-email-channel.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_email_subject
docs.text:
Filter, since 1.4.3. Since 2.0.0 also receives the notification and the instance.

Filters the subject of the email.

$instance holds the resolved settings, secrets included: don't log or dump its settings.

Parameter Type Description $subject string Subject, including the prefix. $notification Notification The notification. $instance Channel_Instance The instance sending it.

Fired in includes/class-notifier.php, modules/email/class-email-channel.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_message_text
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters the plain text of a notification, which channels use as the message.

When a length limit is given to the renderer, the filter may run more than once for one message, and the length is measured on what the filter returns. $notification is then a copy with only the items shown when the message was shortened.

Example, add a line at the end:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_message_text',
    function ( $text, $notification ) {
        return $text . "\n\n-- Sent by my agency";
    },
    10,
    2
);
Parameter Type Description $text string The plain text. $notification Notification The notification it was made from. $hidden int How many items were left out of the text, 0 when none.

Fired in includes/class-notification-renderer.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_more_items_text
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters the line that says how many items were left out of a shortened message.

Return plain text: it is escaped for the format (Markdown, HTML) where needed. The line only exists when at least one item was left out.

Example, say it in another way:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_more_items_text',
    function ( $text, $hidden ) {
        return sprintf( '(%d more not shown)', $hidden );
    },
    10,
    2
);
Parameter Type Description $text string The line, for example "…and 3 more". $hidden int How many items were left out. $notification Notification The notification, with all its items.

Fired in includes/class-notification-renderer.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_notification_failed
docs.text:
Action, since 2.0.0

Fires when delivering a notification through a channel instance failed.

Also fires for an instance that is switched off or whose channel is not available, when a delivery to it was asked for.

A result with a retry_after defers the instance: update checks skip it until then (at most 7 days).

$instance holds the resolved settings, secrets included: don't log or dump its settings.

Parameter Type Description $result Delivery_Result The result, with the reason in its code and message. $notification Notification What was to be delivered. $instance Channel_Instance The instance.

Fired in includes/class-dispatcher.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_notification_sent
docs.text:
Action, since 2.0.0

Fires when a notification was delivered through a channel instance.

$instance holds the resolved settings, secrets included: don't log or dump its settings.

Parameter Type Description $result Delivery_Result The result. $notification Notification What was delivered. $instance Channel_Instance The instance it was delivered through.

Fired in includes/class-dispatcher.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_pre_send
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters a delivery before it happens, to replace it with a result of your own.

Return a Delivery_Result to skip the channel and use that result; any other value sends as normal. Runs for every instance that is switched on and whose channel is available.

Example, hold all deliveries during maintenance:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_pre_send',
    function ( $pre, $notification, $instance ) {
        return my_maintenance_mode()
            ? \WPUN\Delivery_Result::failure( 'Held back.', 'maintenance' )
            : $pre;
    },
    10,
    3
);

$instance holds the resolved settings, secrets included: don't log or dump its settings.

Parameter Type Description $pre null\|Delivery_Result Null. Return a Delivery_Result to short-circuit. $notification Notification What is being delivered. $instance Channel_Instance The instance it is delivered through.

Fired in includes/class-dispatcher.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_channel_deleted
docs.text:
Action, since 2.0.0

Fires after a channel instance was deleted.

$instance holds the resolved settings, secrets included: don't log or dump its settings.

Parameter Type Description $id string Identifier of the deleted instance. $instance Channel_Instance The deleted instance.

Fired in includes/class-channel-store.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_channel_fields
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters the settings fields of a channel type.

The fields are drawn on the add and edit forms, checked by the default Channel::validate_settings() and can be supplied from outside the database. Same schema as Channel::get_fields().

A channel that overrides validate_settings() decides for itself what it keeps, so a field added to it here is drawn but may not be saved. The email channel is one: it keeps only its own fields. Changing the texts of existing fields is always safe.

Example, change the help text of the email channel's recipients:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_channel_fields',
    function ( $fields, $type ) {
        if ( 'email' === $type && isset( $fields['to'] ) ) {
            $fields['to']['description'] = 'Use the team mailing list.';
        }
        return $fields;
    },
    10,
    2
);
Parameter Type Description $fields array<string, array<string, mixed>> The field schemas by name. $type string The channel type.

Fired in includes/abstract-class-channel.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_channel_rejected
docs.text:
Action, since 2.0.0

Fires when a channel is refused because the API version of the site does not satisfy what it needs.

Example:

add_action(
    'sc_wpun_channel_rejected',
    function ( $type, $reason, $channel ) {
        error_log( sprintf( 'Channel "%s" was refused: %s', $type, $reason ) );
    },
    10,
    3
);
Parameter Type Description $type string The channel type. $reason string Why it was refused, as plain text. $channel Channel The channel that was refused.

Fired in includes/class-channel-registry.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_channels
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters the channel instances defined in code.

Starts with the instances of the SC_WPUN_CHANNELS constant. Entries are Channel_Instance objects or arrays with the keys id, type, label, enabled, settings and routing. An instance defined here replaces a stored one with the same id, is read-only in the admin and works like any other for delivery. Invalid entries are reported and skipped.

Example:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_channels',
    function ( $channels ) {
        $channels[] = array(
            'id'       => 'ops_email',
            'type'     => 'email',
            'label'    => 'Operations',
            'enabled'  => true,
            'settings' => array( 'to' => 'ops@example.org' ),
        );
        return $channels;
    }
);
Parameter Type Description $channels array<int\|string, Channel_Instance\|array<string, mixed>> The instances.

Fired in includes/class-channel-store.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_channels_json
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters the JSON text of the SC_WPUN_CHANNELS constant, which defines channel instances in code.

Null when the constant is not defined. A filter can supply the JSON itself, for example from a secrets service. The text is a JSON array of objects with the keys id, type, label, enabled, settings and routing.

Parameter Type Description $json string\|null The JSON text, or null.

Fired in includes/class-channel-store.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_field_types
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters the field types the settings screen can draw and settings can be checked with.

The array is keyed by type. Each entry is an array with a render and a sanitize callable. The built-in types (text, textarea, url, email_list, secret, number, boolean and enum) are in it in the same shape, so an add-on can replace one. checkbox and select are aliases of boolean and enum. An entry that is not an array of two callables is dropped, with a notice to the developer.

render( $field, $name, $id, $value, $disabled, $described_by, $error ) returns the escaped markup of the control. $field is the field schema, $name the name attribute, $id the id, $value the current value, $disabled whether the control is read-only and $described_by the ids of the elements that describe it. $error is the message of an error to show, or an empty string; the error text itself is drawn by the caller, so the control only needs to be marked invalid.

For a field with secret set, $value is '1' when a value is saved and '' when not: the real value is never passed to the callable.

sanitize( $value, $field ) returns the clean value, or a WP_Error when the value is not valid. $field is the field schema, with its name added. The error is reported against the field.

Example, add a colour type:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_field_types',
    function ( $types ) {
        $types['colour'] = array(
            'render'   => function ( $field, $name, $id, $value ) {
                return '<input type="color" id="' . esc_attr( $id ) . '" name="' . esc_attr( $name ) . '" value="' . esc_attr( $value ) . '" />';
            },
            'sanitize' => function ( $value ) {
                return sanitize_hex_color( $value ) ? sanitize_hex_color( $value ) : new WP_Error( 'invalid_colour', 'Enter a colour.' );
            },
        );
        return $types;
    }
);
Parameter Type Description $types array<string, array{render: callable, sanitize: callable}> Field types by name.

Fired in includes/class-field-types.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_register_channels
docs.text:
Action, since 2.0.0

Fires when the notification channels are first needed, for modules and add-ons to register theirs.

Example:

add_action(
    'sc_wpun_register_channels',
    function ( \WPUN\Channel_Registry $registry ) {
        $registry->register( new My_Channel() );
    }
);
Parameter Type Description $registry Channel_Registry The registry to register channels with.

Fired in includes/class-channel-registry.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_config_sources
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters the configuration sources, in the order they are asked.

The first source to return a value wins. By default constants come first, then environment variables if enabled. Add your own to read from a secrets service, or reorder the list. Entries that are not Config_Source objects are dropped.

Example, ask a source of your own after the constants:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_config_sources',
    function ( $sources ) {
        $sources[] = new My_Vault_Source();
        return $sources;
    }
);
Parameter Type Description $sources Config_Source[] The sources.

Fired in includes/class-config.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_config_value
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters the value of a setting or channel field, the last word before the database is used.

Receives what the configuration sources supplied, or null if none did. Return a value to override it, or null to use the saved value from the database. Values are scalars and are cast to the type of the setting or field. Do not log the value: it can be a secret.

Example, take the check frequency from a site option of your own:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_config_value',
    function ( $value, $context, $source ) {
        if ( 'frequency' === $context->get_setting() ) {
            return get_site_option( 'my_frequency', $value );
        }
        return $value;
    },
    10,
    3
);
Parameter Type Description $value string\|bool\|int\|float\|null The value the sources supplied, or null. $context Config_Context What is asked for, and the site. $source string\|null Where the value came from, or null.

Fired in includes/class-config.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_default_settings
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters the settings a new install starts with, and the values used for settings that are missing.

Only the keys below are used, and values are cast to the type shown. Anything else is ignored, as is a return value that is not an array. A notify setting that is not one of its keys falls back to the built-in default.

Example, check daily by default:

add_filter(
    'sc_wpun_default_settings',
    function ( $defaults ) {
        $defaults['frequency'] = 'daily';
        return $defaults;
    }
);
Parameter Type Description $defaults array<string, mixed> The default settings.- string $frequency Name of a cron schedule.- string $notify_core none, all or major (major releases only).- string $notify_plugins none, all or active (active plugins only).- string $notify_themes none, all or active (active themes only).- bool $hide_updates True to hide the WordPress update notice from users who cannot update.

Fired in includes/class-settings.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_get_options_filter
docs.text:
Filter, since 1.4.0

Filters a setting option of the plugin after it is read.

Parameter Type Description $value mixed The stored value. $field string The name of the option.

Fired in includes/class-channel-store.php, includes/class-settings.php, includes/class-state.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_load_from_env
docs.text:
Filter, since 2.0.0

Filters whether configuration is also read from environment variables.

Off unless the environment variable SC_WPUN_LOAD_FROM_ENV is set to an "on" value (1, true, yes or on), so variables a host happens to set never change the plugin's behaviour by surprise.

Parameter Type Description $load_from_env bool Whether to read environment variables.

Fired in includes/class-config.php.

docs.title: sc_wpun_put_options_filter
docs.text:
Filter, since 1.4.0

Filters a setting option of the plugin before it is stored.
